transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-06 14:00 PDT | Duration: 63m | Attendees: Laura Kim, Diego Ramos, Priya Nair (Redwood); Raj Patel (CTO), Maya Chen (ML Eng), Ethan Zhao (Infra)

Summary: Technical deep dive on throughput tuning for BrightScale's on-prem deployment. Discussed continuous batching, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, token caps), KV cache effects on hit rate, quantization impact on latency and perf, and networking/VPC considerations. Next steps and owners at the end.

[00:00] Laura Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, um this is Laura from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, with Diego our SE and Priya who'll help with the pilot ops.
[00:09] Raj Patel: Hey Laura, thanks, we've been waiting to dig into the nitty gritty. Our main ask is to get predictable throughput in our on-prem cluster, right, and keep p99 latency under 200ms for short completions.
[00:19] Diego Ramos: Great, yeah that's the goal we wanted to align on. Quick agenda: continuous batching overview, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch), KV cache sizing and eviction, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem networking tips.
[00:32] Maya Chen: Sounds good, and we have sample workloads — lots of short single-turn inferences, ~8-32 tokens, sometimes bursts up to 256 tokens.
[00:43] Diego Ramos: Okay that's helpful. So first continuous batching: Redwood's runtime keeps an internal queue and builds batches continually rather than fixed interval windows. That means we can get high GPU utilization while keeping latency SLOs by tuning two main knobs: max_num_seqs (limits the number of sequences per batch) and max_tokens_per_batch (or max_total_tokens).
[01:04] Ethan Zhao: Can you explain those knobs in plain — like what's a reasonable starting point?
[01:09] Diego Ramos: Sure. For short token workloads like yours, start with max_num_seqs around 64 per group on an A100-like device, and max_tokens_per_batch maybe 8192. That gives you high parallelism without creating huge padding overhead. If you see latency spikes, reduce max_num_seqs to 32 and increase the timer threshold slightly.
[01:25] Raj Patel: Timer threshold? We didn't see that in the docs.
[01:28] Priya Nair: Right, there's also a micro-timer that flushes partial batches after N ms to avoid unbounded latency; it's commonly set at 10-30ms. So knobs to watch: max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch, and the flush timer (batch_timeout_ms).
[01:42] Maya Chen: Makes sense. What about continuous vs periodic batching — are there tradeoffs?
[01:46] Diego Ramos: Yes. Continuous batching is lower latency for bursty traffic since it builds batches as requests arrive; periodic (fixed-window) can be simpler but tends to either add latency or reduce throughput depending on window size. We recommend continuous for production interactive APIs.
[02:00] Raj Patel: You mentioned padding overhead — can you quantify that?
[02:04] Diego Ramos: Padding cost depends on sequence length variance. If most requests are 8 tokens but you pad to the longest sequence in the batch, you waste compute. Two mitigations: bucket by length pre-batching, or use max_tokens_per_batch so large sequences don't force small ones to pad too much. Also KV cache prefix caching helps when you have repeat prompts.
[02:22] Maya Chen: Tell us more about KV cache sizing — we've seen memory blowouts in our first pass.
[02:27] Diego Ramos: Yeah, KV cache is per-token per-layer state. For long context windows it can be large. On GPUs, we recommend keeping per-request max_prompt_tokens and LRU eviction; Redwood's runtime supports prefix/KV caching with configurable eviction policies. For BrightScale I'd set a per-client cache budget and an eviction window of 10k tokens initially.
[02:46] Ethan Zhao: Are evictions sync'd across replicas? We run a multi-replica pool.
[02:51] Priya Nair: Eviction is local per-replica; if you want global consistency you can front KV lookups with a small shard-aware cache layer or use sticky routing to a replica so hot clients hit the same cache. That's a tradeoff: sticky routing gives better hit rate but reduces flexibility for autoscaling.
[03:08] Raj Patel: Hmm okay. Also curious about quantization — how much latency do we gain versus accuracy loss for our models?
[03:15] Diego Ramos: For 8-bit quant, on many LLMs you typically get 15-25% lower memory footprint and 10-30% throughput improvement depending on kernels. Accuracy can drop slightly on edge tasks; we recommend running per-task evals. 4-bit can yield bigger gains but needs compatible kernels and may affect int8/int4 fusing. We can provide model-specific profiles.
[03:38] Maya Chen: Do we need special hardware or kernels for 4-bit?
[03:41] Diego Ramos: Yes, some 4-bit optimizations rely on custom fused kernels; our runtime includes options for quant kernels and will auto-select based on model config and device capability. If you're on older drivers you might see falls back to slower paths.
[03:55] Ethan Zhao: What about p99 outliers — sometimes we get a single request that takes 2s while typical is 80ms.
[04:01] Diego Ramos: Common causes: huge sequence length in the batch, KV cache miss leading to cold loads, or a preemption/GC on the host. Mitigations: enforce max_token_per_request, add admission control to route large requests to a lower-priority queue, and ensure GPU affinity to avoid preemption.
[04:20] Raj Patel: Could you walk through an example config?
[04:23] Diego Ramos: Sure, example for A100 80GB serving short-turns: max_num_seqs=48, max_total_tokens=8192, batch_timeout_ms=20, max_request_tokens=1024, cache_eviction_tokens=10000. For bursty high conc you can bump max_num_seqs to 128 but increase padding and watch latency.
[04:42] Maya Chen: For our on-prem, we have mixed devices — some A10s and a few A100s, how does scheduler handle heterogeneous fleets?
[04:50] Priya Nair: Redwood scheduler routes by device profile; you can tag pools (high-priority A100 pool, cost-optimized A10 pool). For latency-sensitive routes pin to A100. There's also automatic fallback: if A100 pool is saturated it can route to A10 pool with a lower SLO.
[05:06] Ethan Zhao: How does the runtime decide to prefer fewer big batches vs more small batches? Is that purely based on those knobs?
[05:11] Diego Ramos: It's driven by the knobs and an internal utility function that estimates expected latency vs throughput given current queue depth and sequence length distribution. We expose the main knobs so you don't need to tune the utility directly.
[05:23] Raj Patel: Are there monitoring signals you recommend?
[05:26] Diego Ramos: Yes — batch sizes histogram, padding ratio, KV cache hit rate, GPU utilization, per-route token throughput, and queue latency percentiles. Those help you correlate tuning changes with results.
[05:37] Maya Chen: We saw some odd token accounting — our token meter shows lower tokens served than our client logs.
[05:43] Laura Kim: That often comes from streaming partial tokens or function-calling additional tokens; ensure client is counting prompts+completions and that streaming doesn't double-count on retries. We can help map metrics.
[05:55] Ethan Zhao: About VPC/on-prem network overhead — do you see TLS and NICS making big differences?
[05:59] Priya Nair: For high throughput microsecond-sensitive workloads, NIC offload and kernel-bypass (e.g., DPDK) can shave tens of microseconds. More commonly you see few ms in TLS and ingress egress; use local grpcs and colocate inference inside the same AZ or on-prem rack.
[06:14] Raj Patel: For our security team, they want audit logs and KMS integration on the private plane. Is that supported?
[06:19] Laura Kim: Yes — Redwood Private supports customer KMS/HSM, audit logs, SSO, and SOC 2 controls. We'll share the security pack — it's in the next steps.
[06:28] Maya Chen: Back to scheduling — what's max_num_seqs interaction with model parallelism? If a model is sharded across GPUs, does batch size need to align?
[06:35] Diego Ramos: For model parallelism you want balanced micro-batches per shard; Redwood's runtime coordinates across replicas to shard batch tensors. The effective batch per device matters, so max_num_seqs should be set so per-shard batch isn't too small; otherwise overhead rises. We'll provide guidelines per model type (e.g., 7B vs 70B).
[06:51] Raj Patel: Any gotchas if we do sticky routing to improve KV hit rates?
[06:55] Diego Ramos: Sticky routing helps KV but reduces autoscaling elasticity — hot shards can become overloaded. A hybrid approach: short sticky windows (a few minutes) plus global autoscaler works well. Also monitor per-replica load.
[07:07] Maya Chen: Let's talk expected numbers — once tuned, what's throughput per A100 for our workload?
[07:11] Diego Ramos: For short 8-32 token completions on a single A100 you might see tens of thousands of requests per minute — roughly 600-2k rps depending on model and quant. We'll validate with a benchmark.
[07:23] Raj Patel: Good. Anything else on quantization?
[07:26] Diego Ramos: Just that kernel selection matters; some fused kernels can make quantized runs faster than float even at small batch sizes. We'll include kernel mapping in the runbook.
[07:36] Priya Nair: Quick ops note — for on-prem pilot we'll want host metrics (GPU ECC errors, driver versions), container runtime, and the initial test harness. We'll template that in the runbook.
[07:47] Maya Chen: Ok thanks. Can you also include recommended default admission control policies?
[07:52] Diego Ramos: Yes: reject-or-queue when request_tokens > max_request_tokens, route to low-priority queue for requests > 256 tokens, and cap burst concurrency per API key.
[08:05] Laura Kim: Alright, let's recap next steps — Laura will share runbook and security pack; Diego will run a benchmark using BrightScale sample prompts and share results; team to schedule pilot kickoff for 10/20.
[08:16] Raj Patel: That works. Anyone want to add items?
[08:19] Ethan Zhao: I'll share our cluster inventory and driver versions.
[08:21] Maya Chen: I'll upload sample prompt sets and target SLAs.
[08:24] Laura Kim: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in the CRM and send calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.

End of transcript.
